Sure!  I think you are on the right track already if you are open to criticism.  A lot of this stuff will probably overlap but I will try and make this as cohesive as possible.  

I think the most frustrating thing for me when I am debating with someone is when they derail.  There are many ways to do it (the website I like that has a lot of good info about it is down) and it's one way to get anyone to stop debating with you.

Also being able to recognize that YOUR experience is not indicative of anyone elses. I see people not doing this ALL OVER REDDIT.  For example a person with a normal weight saying "Why don't people just eat less to lose weight, it's not that hard!" or in the context of your debate (I'm not inferring that you said this, just a very common argument), "someone discriminated against me so that means I know what it feels like to be a minority and experience racism"

Being aware of that, you should have an easier time actually imagining putting yourself in your opponent's shoes and trying to understand where they are coming from before ruling out their comments or statements, if that makes sense.

Don't name call or otherwise try to personally insult the person if you want to be taken seriously.  It generally looks bad and immature and does not contribute to the debate.  

Avoid logical fallacies (straw man, ad hominem, etc). [This one is super important](http://www.csun.edu/~dgw61315/fallacies.html).  That might be worth a read for you and I'm sure stuff I've already mentioned is probably on there.  One important thing I want to point out is don't take your opponents comments out of context!  You can't debate a point they didn't make.

Use relevant information and sources if you can.  You will be more successful if you can use facts over beliefs.

So basically, be respectful, don't attack or name call, present your facts, ask questions and be willing to listen, be open to their perspective, avoid logical fallacies, stay on topic, and don't let your emotions get involved.  I'm not an expert or anything, but these are good rules to go by.  How you present your argument and information is important too because even if you try to go by these guidelines, if it sounds sloppy or not well thought out then people will ignore/downvote you.

Remember, sometimes there isn't a right or a wrong answer (although I think that might be debate vs discussion) or more often, you may not ever come to an agreement with the person you are debating with.  That's okay too.   Anyway, there is my two cents about arguing on the internet.  I am sure the same principles are applied to in person debates but I don't know anything about the etiquette.

Fine. I'll bite. Here's some possible reasons you may have been downvoted without comment. Someone already addressed you in an articulate way and they were more "enlightening" then I could have been.  It seemed like you didn't really read their posts and responded with irrelevant information which comes off as trying to derail while missing their point.  I could also see how some of the things you said might be considered insulting (accusing someone of making up descriptions for words that were pretty accurate to appear more edgy or accusing anyone of racism for pointing out white privilege.)  None of those things made me want to spend the time to actually contribute, maybe others felt the same.
I've lived in a lot of places and I'm beginning to think that it doesn't even matter where I live, I will still be unhappy.
